UNINCORPORATED NONPROFIT ASSOCIATION — FORMATION AND MEMBER LIABILITY INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Sunset Terrace Owners Association · providing after-school educational programs to underserved youth

UNINCORPORATED NONPROFIT ASSOCIATION — INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE
This information sheet describes, in general terms, how California law treats an unincorporated nonprofit association under Title 3 of the Corporations Code (Corp. Code §§ 18000–24001.5), which governs unincorporated associations generally, and Part 2 of that title (Corp. Code §§ 18605–21401), which contains provisions specific to nonprofit associations. It concerns Sunset Terrace Owners Association, an unincorporated group formed for the common purpose described as providing after-school educational programs to underserved youth. This sheet addresses the statutory definition of an unincorporated association and a nonprofit association, the statutory rule on personal liability of members, directors, officers, and agents for the association's own debts and obligations, and the association's statutory capacity to hold property and to sue or be sued in its own name. It does not address incorporation as a nonprofit corporation under a different part of the Corporations Code, tax-exempt status under state or federal law, or the Attorney General's charitable-trust registration requirements for an association that holds property for charitable purposes, each of which — where covered at all — is addressed in a separate document in this library. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself form, dissolve, or alter the governance of any association, and it does not determine whether Sunset Terrace Owners Association or any other group meets the statutory definition of an unincorporated association or a nonprofit association on its particular facts.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF UNINCORPORATED ASSOCIATION AND NONPROFIT ASSOCIATION
California's Corporations Code defines the terms used throughout Title 3's provisions on unincorporated associations. By statute, "‘Unincorporated association’ means an unincorporated group of two or more persons joined by mutual consent for a common lawful purpose, whether organized for profit or not." The same section states that certain arrangements do not, by themselves, create an unincorporated association: joint tenancy, tenancy in common, community property, or other property co-ownership does not establish an unincorporated association merely because the co-owners share a common purpose, and neither does marriage or a registered domestic partnership. Within that broader category, the statute defines a narrower one: "‘Nonprofit association’ means an unincorporated association with a primary common purpose other than to operate a business for profit," and the statute clarifies that such an association may still carry on a business for profit and apply the resulting profit to any activity in which it may lawfully engage. The statute also fixes the meaning of "member": where an association's own governing principles define its membership, that definition controls; where they do not, a person is a member if, under the association's governing principles, that person "has a right to participate in the selection of persons authorized to manage the affairs of the unincorporated association or in the development of policy of the unincorporated association, but does not include a person who participates solely as director, officer, or agent of the association."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Unincorporated association” means an unincorporated group of two or more persons joined by mutual consent for a common lawful purpose, whether organized for profit or not."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18035(a), Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, statutory definition of "unincorporated association" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18035.)
  "“Nonprofit association” means an unincorporated association with a primary common purpose other than to operate a business for profit."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18020(a), Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, statutory definition of "nonprofit association" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18020.)
  "“member” means a person who, pursuant to the governing principles of the unincorporated association, has a right to participate in the selection of persons authorized to manage the affairs of the unincorporated association or in the development of policy of the unincorporated association, but does not include a person who participates solely as director, officer, or agent of the association."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18015(b), Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, default statutory definition of "member" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18015.)
  Known gap: These definitions govern Title 3's general provisions on unincorporated associations, which by their own terms do not apply to a corporation, a government or governmental subdivision or agency, a partnership or joint venture, a limited liability company, or a labor organization governed by a constitution or bylaws (Corp. Code § 18055); this clause does not quote § 18055's exclusion list itself. It also does not address the separate definitions used for a specific kind of unincorporated group elsewhere in California law — for example, a homeowners association under the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act (Civ. Code § 4000 et seq.) or a cooperative corporation — both of which appear only incidentally, and for unrelated purposes, in other documents already in this corpus. Whether a particular group's arrangement satisfies the "mutual consent for a common lawful purpose" standard, or whether its own governing principles define "member" differently from the statutory default, are fact-specific questions this clause does not resolve.

PERSONAL LIABILITY OF MEMBERS, DIRECTORS, AND AGENTS FOR ASSOCIATION DEBTS
California's Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act states a general rule shielding individuals from an association's own debts: "A member, director, or agent of a nonprofit association is not liable for a debt, obligation, or liability of the association solely by reason of being a member, director, officer, or agent." This codifies a principle California courts had already recognized at common law: one Court of Appeal decision, quoting earlier authority, stated that "[a] member of an unincorporated association does not incur liability for acts of the association or acts of its members which he did not authorize or perform." The statutory shield is not unconditional. The same chapter separately makes a member, director, officer, or agent liable for injury, damage, or harm caused by an act or omission of the association, or of one of its directors, officers, or agents, where the individual expressly assumes liability for the conduct, personally engages in tortious conduct causing the harm, or is otherwise liable under some other statute; the statute describes this as "a nonexclusive list of existing grounds for liability, and does not foreclose any common law grounds for liability." The chapter also preserves common-law alter-ego exposure: "a member or person in control of a nonprofit association may be subject to liability for a debt, obligation, or liability of the association under common law principles governing alter ego liability of shareholders of a corporation, taking into account the differences between a nonprofit association and a corporation."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A member, director, or agent of a nonprofit association is not liable for a debt, obligation, or liability of the association solely by reason of being a member, director, officer, or agent."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18605, Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, general rule against personal liability solely from membership or office (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18605.)
  "A member, director, officer, or agent of a nonprofit association shall be liable for injury, damage, or harm caused by an act or omission of the association or an act or omission of a director, officer, or agent of the association, if any of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) The member, director, officer, or agent expressly assumes liability for injury, damage, or harm caused by particular conduct and that conduct causes the injury, damage, or harm. (2) The member, director, officer, or agent engages in tortious conduct that causes the injury, damage, or harm. (3) The member, director, officer, or agent is otherwise liable under any other statute."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18620(a), Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, statutory grounds for individual liability for injury, damage, or harm (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18620.)
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter, a member or person in control of a nonprofit association may be subject to liability for a debt, obligation, or liability of the association under common law principles governing alter ego liability of shareholders of a corporation, taking into account the differences between a nonprofit association and a corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18630, Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, preservation of common-law alter-ego liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18630.)
  "[a] member of an unincorporated association does not incur liability for acts of the association or acts of its members which he did not authorize or perform."
  — Heiman v. Workers' Compensation Appeals Board, 149 Cal. App. 4th 724 (2007), 149 Cal. App. 4th 724, 734 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2276075/heiman-v-workers-compensation-appeals-board/)
  Known gap: This chapter's protection runs against liability "solely by reason of" status as a member, director, or officer; it does not immunize a person for conduct falling within § 18620(a)'s own exceptions, for alter-ego liability under § 18630, or for a contractual obligation the person personally assumes or ratifies under § 18610, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document. The Heiman decision cited here applied the underlying no-personal-liability-for-unauthorized-acts principle in the context of a homeowners association member's potential status as an "employer" for workers' compensation purposes, drawing on Corp. Code § 18250's general rule that an association is liable for its own and its agents' acts to the same extent as a natural person, rather than on § 18605 itself; it is cited here only because it states and applies the same common-law principle that § 18605 codifies for nonprofit associations specifically, not because it interprets § 18605. Whether a particular member, director, or agent's conduct falls within one of § 18620(a)'s exceptions, or satisfies the alter-ego factors referenced in § 18630, are fact-specific determinations this clause does not make.

WHEN A MEMBER, DIRECTOR, OFFICER, OR AGENT MAY BE LIABLE ON THE ASSOCIATION'S CONTRACTS
The general no-personal-liability rule for a nonprofit association's obligations has a separate, more detailed counterpart for contracts. By statute, "A member of a nonprofit association is not liable for a contractual obligation of the association unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) The member expressly assumes personal responsibility for the obligation in a signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed. (b) The member expressly authorizes or ratifies the specific contract, as evidenced by a writing. This subdivision does not apply if the member authorizes or ratifies a contract solely in the member's capacity as a director, officer, or agent of the association. (c) With notice of the contract, the member receives a benefit under the contract. Liability under this subdivision is limited to the value of the benefit received. (d) The member executes the contract without disclosing that the member is acting on behalf of the association. (e) The member executes the contract without authority to execute the contract." A parallel statute states a similar rule for a director, officer, or agent, conditioned on a narrower set of three circumstances: "A director, officer, or agent of a nonprofit association is not liable for a contractual obligation of the association unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) The director, officer, or agent expressly assumes responsibility for the obligation in a signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed. (b) The director, officer, or agent executes the contract without disclosing that the director, officer, or agent is acting on behalf of the association. (c) The director, officer, or agent executes the contract without authority to execute the contract." Apart from these specific rules, general agency law fills the gaps: "Except to the extent this title provides a specific rule, the general law of agency ... applies to an unincorporated association."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A member of a nonprofit association is not liable for a contractual obligation of the association unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) The member expressly assumes personal responsibility for the obligation in a signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed. (b) The member expressly authorizes or ratifies the specific contract, as evidenced by a writing. This subdivision does not apply if the member authorizes or ratifies a contract solely in the member’s capacity as a director, officer, or agent of the association. (c) With notice of the contract, the member receives a benefit under the contract. Liability under this subdivision is limited to the value of the benefit received. (d) The member executes the contract without disclosing that the member is acting on behalf of the association. (e) The member executes the contract without authority to execute the contract."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18610, Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, conditions for a member's contractual liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18610.)
  "A director, officer, or agent of a nonprofit association is not liable for a contractual obligation of the association unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) The director, officer, or agent expressly assumes responsibility for the obligation in a signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed. (b) The director, officer, or agent executes the contract without disclosing that the director, officer, or agent is acting on behalf of the association. (c) The director, officer, or agent executes the contract without authority to execute the contract."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18615, Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, conditions for a director's, officer's, or agent's contractual liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18615.)
  "Except to the extent this title provides a specific rule, the general law of agency, including Article 2 (commencing with Section 2019) of Chapter 2 of Title 6 of, and Title 9 (commencing with Section 2295) of, Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code, applies to an unincorporated association."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18065, Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, general law of agency applies except where this title provides a specific rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18065.)
  Known gap: These two statutes were enacted together in 2004 and, unlike § 18605's blanket shield, apply specifically to an association's contractual obligations. They differ from each other in one respect: only the member-liability statute (§ 18610) includes a receipt-of-benefit ground (subdivision (c)); the director/officer/agent statute (§ 18615) does not. Both statutes turn on fact-specific questions — whether a writing satisfies the "signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed" standard, what counts as "ratification" of a specific contract, or whether a person disclosed that they were acting on the association's behalf — that this clause does not resolve for any particular contract. This clause quotes § 18065's cross-reference to general agency law only in part, omitting the specific Civil Code article and title citations it names; it does not itself state what that general agency law requires for a particular officer's authority to bind the association, which depends on the association's own governing documents and on the agency-law provisions § 18065 references.

CAPACITY TO HOLD PROPERTY AND TO SUE OR BE SUED IN THE ASSOCIATION'S OWN NAME
Because an unincorporated association is not a natural person or a corporation, California law states expressly that it may nonetheless act, and be dealt with, in its own name. By statute, "An unincorporated association may, in its name, acquire, hold, manage, encumber, or transfer an interest in real or personal property." Property obtained this way belongs to the association itself, not to its members individually: "Property acquired by or for an unincorporated association is property of the unincorporated association and not of the members individually." A separate statute, in the Code of Civil Procedure, gives an unincorporated association the same kind of standing in litigation: "A partnership or other unincorporated association, whether organized for profit or not, may sue and be sued in the name it has assumed or by which it is known." Acquiring, transferring, or encumbering an interest in real property specifically must be executed in a defined way: "The acquisition, transfer, or encumbrance of an interest in real property by an unincorporated association shall be executed by its president and secretary or other comparable officers, or by a person specifically designated by a resolution adopted by the association, or by a committee or other body or person authorized to act by the governing principles of the association."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An unincorporated association may, in its name, acquire, hold, manage, encumber, or transfer an interest in real or personal property."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18105, Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, capacity to acquire, hold, and transfer property in the association's own name (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18105.)
  "Property acquired by or for an unincorporated association is property of the unincorporated association and not of the members individually."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18110, Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, association property is not the members' individual property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18110.)
  "The acquisition, transfer, or encumbrance of an interest in real property by an unincorporated association shall be executed by its president and secretary or other comparable officers, or by a person specifically designated by a resolution adopted by the association, or by a committee or other body or person authorized to act by the governing principles of the association."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18115, Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, execution requirements for real property transactions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18115.)
  "A partnership or other unincorporated association, whether organized for profit or not, may sue and be sued in the name it has assumed or by which it is known."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 369.5(a), Capacity of a partnership or unincorporated association to sue and be sued in its assumed or known name (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=369.5.)
  Known gap: Sections 18105 and 18115's property-holding rules and § 369.5's litigation capacity are general default rules; a statute governing a particular kind of association — for example, the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's rules for a homeowners association, addressed elsewhere in this corpus, or the Cooperative Corporation Law — can supply a different rule that prevails to the extent of any inconsistency (Corp. Code § 18060). Code of Civil Procedure § 369.5 has a second subdivision, not quoted here, that separately allows a member to be joined as a party in a suit against the association and addresses how a judgment against that individual member may be obtained in that same action; this clause addresses only the association's own capacity to sue and be sued in its name, not that separate joinder mechanism. Nothing quoted in this clause itself transfers title to any specific property into an association's name, creates or dissolves the association, or determines who currently holds signing authority on the association's behalf — those depend on the association's own governing documents and, for real property, on the recorded instrument itself.

LIMITS ON ENFORCING A JUDGMENT AGAINST THE ASSOCIATION'S MEMBERS
California law also states how a money judgment against an unincorporated association may be enforced, and limits when a judgment based on the association's own liability can instead be enforced against an individual member, director, officer, or agent. By statute, "A money judgment against an unincorporated association, whether organized for profit or not, may be enforced only against the property of the association." A related statute extends this protection to individuals in most circumstances: "A judgment creditor of a member, director, officer, or agent of an unincorporated association may not levy execution against the assets of the member, director, officer, or agent to satisfy a judgment based on a claim against the unincorporated association unless a judgment based on the same claim has been obtained against the unincorporated association and any of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) A writ of execution on the judgment against the unincorporated association has been returned unsatisfied in whole or in part. (2) The unincorporated association is a debtor in bankruptcy. (3) The member, director, officer, or agent has agreed that the creditor need not exhaust the assets of the unincorporated association. (4) A court grants permission to the judgment creditor to levy execution against the assets of a member, director, officer, or agent based on a finding that the assets of the unincorporated association subject to execution are clearly insufficient to satisfy the judgment, that exhaustion of the assets of the unincorporated association is excessively burdensome, or that the grant of permission is an appropriate exercise of the court's equitable powers." This exhaustion requirement applies only to a claim against the individual that is itself based on a claim against the association: "Nothing in this section affects the right of a judgment creditor to levy execution against the assets of a member, director, officer, or agent of an unincorporated association if the claim against the member, director, officer, or agent is not based on a claim against the unincorporated association."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A money judgment against an unincorporated association, whether organized for profit or not, may be enforced only against the property of the association."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18260, Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, a money judgment against the association reaches only association property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18260.)
  "A judgment creditor of a member, director, officer, or agent of an unincorporated association may not levy execution against the assets of the member, director, officer, or agent to satisfy a judgment based on a claim against the unincorporated association unless a judgment based on the same claim has been obtained against the unincorporated association and any of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) A writ of execution on the judgment against the unincorporated association has been returned unsatisfied in whole or in part. (2) The unincorporated association is a debtor in bankruptcy. (3) The member, director, officer, or agent has agreed that the creditor need not exhaust the assets of the unincorporated association. (4) A court grants permission to the judgment creditor to levy execution against the assets of a member, director, officer, or agent based on a finding that the assets of the unincorporated association subject to execution are clearly insufficient to satisfy the judgment, that exhaustion of the assets of the unincorporated association is excessively burdensome, or that the grant of permission is an appropriate exercise of the court’s equitable powers."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18270(a), Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, conditions under which a judgment creditor may levy against an individual member's or officer's assets (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18270.)
  "Nothing in this section affects the right of a judgment creditor to levy execution against the assets of a member, director, officer, or agent of an unincorporated association if the claim against the member, director, officer, or agent is not based on a claim against the unincorporated association."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 18270(b), Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, the exhaustion requirement does not limit a creditor's independent claim against the individual (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=18270.)
  Known gap: These enforcement limits are procedurally separate from the substantive liability rules in Corp. Code §§ 18605–18630: a member may already be substantively liable on some independent ground — for example, under § 18610's contract-liability exceptions or § 18620's tort-liability exceptions, each addressed in a separate clause of this document — and still benefit from § 18270(a)'s requirement that a creditor first obtain, and attempt to enforce, a judgment against the association itself unless one of § 18270(a)'s four listed conditions is met. Corp. Code § 18250, not quoted in this clause, separately makes the association itself liable for its own and its agents' acts or omissions to the same extent as a natural person; this clause addresses only how a resulting judgment may then be enforced, not the association's own underlying liability. Whether a judgment creditor has satisfied one of § 18270(a)'s conditions, or whether a specific claim against an individual is "based on" a claim against the association within the meaning of § 18270(b), are fact-specific determinations this clause does not make.

Whether a particular member, director, or agent's conduct falls within one of § 18620(a)'s exceptions, or satisfies the alter-ego factors referenced in § 18630, are fact-specific determinations this clause does not make.

expectedJSON.body: The general no-personal-liability rule for a nonprofit association's obligations has a separate, more detailed counterpart for contracts. By statute, "A member of a nonprofit association is not liable for a contractual obligation of the association unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) The member expressly assumes personal responsibility for the obligation in a signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed. (b) The member expressly authorizes or ratifies the specific contract, as evidenced by a writing. This subdivision does not apply if the member authorizes or ratifies a contract solely in the member's capacity as a director, officer, or agent of the association. (c) With notice of the contract, the member receives a benefit under the contract. Liability under this subdivision is limited to the value of the benefit received. (d) The member executes the contract without disclosing that the member is acting on behalf of the association. (e) The member executes the contract without authority to execute the contract." A parallel statute states a similar rule for a director, officer, or agent, conditioned on a narrower set of three circumstances: "A director, officer, or agent of a nonprofit association is not liable for a contractual obligation of the association unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) The director, officer, or agent expressly assumes responsibility for the obligation in a signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed. (b) The director, officer, or agent executes the contract without disclosing that the director, officer, or agent is acting on behalf of the association. (c) The director, officer, or agent executes the contract without authority to execute the contract." Apart from these specific rules, general agency law fills the gaps: "Except to the extent this title provides a specific rule, the general law of agency ... applies to an unincorporated association."

expectedJSON.gap: These two statutes were enacted together in 2004 and, unlike § 18605's blanket shield, apply specifically to an association's contractual obligations. They differ from each other in one respect: only the member-liability statute (§ 18610) includes a receipt-of-benefit ground (subdivision (c)); the director/officer/agent statute (§ 18615) does not. Both statutes turn on fact-specific questions — whether a writing satisfies the "signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed" standard, what counts as "ratification" of a specific contract, or whether a person disclosed that they were acting on the association's behalf — that this clause does not resolve for any particular contract. This clause quotes § 18065's cross-reference to general agency law only in part, omitting the specific Civil Code article and title citations it names; it does not itself state what that general agency law requires for a particular officer's authority to bind the association, which depends on the association's own governing documents and on the agency-law provisions § 18065 references.

expectedJSON.body: Because an unincorporated association is not a natural person or a corporation, California law states expressly that it may nonetheless act, and be dealt with, in its own name. By statute, "An unincorporated association may, in its name, acquire, hold, manage, encumber, or transfer an interest in real or personal property." Property obtained this way belongs to the association itself, not to its members individually: "Property acquired by or for an unincorporated association is property of the unincorporated association and not of the members individually." A separate statute, in the Code of Civil Procedure, gives an unincorporated association the same kind of standing in litigation: "A partnership or other unincorporated association, whether organized for profit or not, may sue and be sued in the name it has assumed or by which it is known." Acquiring, transferring, or encumbering an interest in real property specifically must be executed in a defined way: "The acquisition, transfer, or encumbrance of an interest in real property by an unincorporated association shall be executed by its president and secretary or other comparable officers, or by a person specifically designated by a resolution adopted by the association, or by a committee or other body or person authorized to act by the governing principles of the association."

expectedJSON.gap: Sections 18105 and 18115's property-holding rules and § 369.5's litigation capacity are general default rules; a statute governing a particular kind of association — for example, the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's rules for a homeowners association, addressed elsewhere in this corpus, or the Cooperative Corporation Law — can supply a different rule that prevails to the extent of any inconsistency (Corp. Code § 18060). Code of Civil Procedure § 369.5 has a second subdivision, not quoted here, that separately allows a member to be joined as a party in a suit against the association and addresses how a judgment against that individual member may be obtained in that same action; this clause addresses only the association's own capacity to sue and be sued in its name, not that separate joinder mechanism. Nothing quoted in this clause itself transfers title to any specific property into an association's name, creates or dissolves the association, or determines who currently holds signing authority on the association's behalf — those depend on the association's own governing documents and, for real property, on the recorded instrument itself.

expectedJSON.body: California law also states how a money judgment against an unincorporated association may be enforced, and limits when a judgment based on the association's own liability can instead be enforced against an individual member, director, officer, or agent. By statute, "A money judgment against an unincorporated association, whether organized for profit or not, may be enforced only against the property of the association." A related statute extends this protection to individuals in most circumstances: "A judgment creditor of a member, director, officer, or agent of an unincorporated association may not levy execution against the assets of the member, director, officer, or agent to satisfy a judgment based on a claim against the unincorporated association unless a judgment based on the same claim has been obtained against the unincorporated association and any of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) A writ of execution on the judgment against the unincorporated association has been returned unsatisfied in whole or in part. (2) The unincorporated association is a debtor in bankruptcy. (3) The member, director, officer, or agent has agreed that the creditor need not exhaust the assets of the unincorporated association. (4) A court grants permission to the judgment creditor to levy execution against the assets of a member, director, officer, or agent based on a finding that the assets of the unincorporated association subject to execution are clearly insufficient to satisfy the judgment, that exhaustion of the assets of the unincorporated association is excessively burdensome, or that the grant of permission is an appropriate exercise of the court's equitable powers." This exhaustion requirement applies only to a claim against the individual that is itself based on a claim against the association: "Nothing in this section affects the right of a judgment creditor to levy execution against the assets of a member, director, officer, or agent of an unincorporated association if the claim against the member, director, officer, or agent is not based on a claim against the unincorporated association."

(2) The unincorporated association is a debtor in bankruptcy. (3) The member, director, officer, or agent has agreed that the creditor need not exhaust the assets of the unincorporated association. (4) A court grants permission to the judgment creditor to levy execution against the assets of a member, director, officer, or agent based on a finding that the assets of the unincorporated association subject to execution are clearly insufficient to satisfy the judgment, that exhaustion of the assets of the unincorporated association is excessively burdensome, or that the grant of permission is an appropriate exercise of the court’s equitable powers.

expectedJSON.gap: These enforcement limits are procedurally separate from the substantive liability rules in Corp. Code §§ 18605–18630: a member may already be substantively liable on some independent ground — for example, under § 18610's contract-liability exceptions or § 18620's tort-liability exceptions, each addressed in a separate clause of this document — and still benefit from § 18270(a)'s requirement that a creditor first obtain, and attempt to enforce, a judgment against the association itself unless one of § 18270(a)'s four listed conditions is met. Corp. Code § 18250, not quoted in this clause, separately makes the association itself liable for its own and its agents' acts or omissions to the same extent as a natural person; this clause addresses only how a resulting judgment may then be enforced, not the association's own underlying liability. Whether a judgment creditor has satisfied one of § 18270(a)'s conditions, or whether a specific claim against an individual is "based on" a claim against the association within the meaning of § 18270(b), are fact-specific determinations this clause does not make.
